study_identification_part.si4_title: Multivariate brain-cognition associations in euthymic bipolar disorder

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To examine multivariate associations between cortical thickness and core cognitive functions (processing speed, attention, and executive function) in euthymic bipolar disorder using normative models of cortical thickness and canonical correlation analysis.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) was used to assess multivariate associations between neuropsychological performance (7 variables: d2 CP, d2 %Error, d2 FR, DSST minus Symbol Copy, TMT-A, TMT-B minus TMT-A, Category Fluency) and cortical thickness (23 principal components explaining 90% of variance across 68 ROIs) in the BD group. Principal Components Analysis (PCA) was first applied to cortical thickness data to reduce dimensionality. Statistical significance tested using Pillai's trace and permutation test (10,000 permutations). Loadings and cross-loadings with coefficients above 0.3 or below -0.3 were considered non-trivial. The first canonical correlation was strong (rho=0.860) but did not reach statistical significance (Pillai's trace p=0.112; permutation test p=0.093). Group differences in cognitive performance and cortical thickness were tested using Student's t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons (FDR 5%).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: BD showed impairments in processing speed and executive function tests (DSST, TMT-B) associated with abnormal cortical thickness in left inferior temporal, right entorhinal, and right temporal pole areas, though the canonical correlation did not reach statistical significance (rho=0.860, p=0.093).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Euthymic BD patients (n=56) showed significantly poorer performance than matched controls (n=26) on tests of processing speed (DSST minus Symbol Copy: Cohen's d=0.77, p<.001), attention (d2 CP: d=0.60, p=.008; d2 %Error: d=0.63, p=.026), and executive function (Category Fluency: d=0.47, p=.030) after controlling for age and premorbid IQ, with medium to large effect sizes. BD patients also showed reduced cortical thickness compared to normative controls (n=5977) in multiple regions, with medium effect sizes for left postcentral (d=0.645), precentral (d=0.645), paracentral (d=0.574), and caudal middle frontal areas (d=0.520), and small effect sizes for bilateral parietal and frontal regions and right insula (d>0.2). Canonical correlation analysis revealed a strong but non-significant association (rho=0.860, Pillai's trace p=0.112, permutation p=0.093) between cognitive impairments and cortical thickness. The cognitive canonical variate was most strongly loaded by DSST (loading=-0.675, cross-loading=-0.580) and TMT-B minus TMT-A (loading=0.353, cross-loading=0.303). Cortical thickness in left inferior temporal (rho=0.406, p=.002), right entorhinal (rho=0.380, p=.004), and right temporal pole (rho=0.334, p=.012) showed the strongest cross-loadings with the cognitive canonical variate, suggesting these temporal regions may be particularly associated with processing speed and executive function impairments in euthymic BD. No significant differences in cortical thickness were found between BD patients taking lithium (n=29, 52%) and those naïve to lithium.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: This study demonstrates the utility of combining normative modeling with large public datasets and multivariate methods (CCA) to examine brain-cognition associations in mood disorders. The normative modeling approach mitigated limitations of small control sample by using large multi-site reference data (n=5977 from 5 datasets) while accounting for scanner/site differences. The matched controls were only needed to estimate site-specific offsets for harmonization. Future research should continue to leverage normative modeling and multivariate approaches, may benefit from exploring covariance between cortical morphological metrics (thickness, volume, surface area) using independent components approaches, and should include larger samples to enable proper cross-validation and achieve adequate statistical power for detecting multivariate brain-cognition associations.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Modest BD sample size (n=56) limiting statistical power for CCA (some recommend n≥20 times number of variables); sample too small for train/test split cross-validation; first canonical correlation did not reach statistical significance (p=0.093) requiring cautious interpretation; limited neuropsychological battery not assessing working memory, verbal memory, or visuospatial processing; lack of computerized sustained attention measures; cognitive heterogeneity within BD group not fully addressed; clinical confounds (illness duration, severity, BD type I/II, psychosis) not controlled due to limited power; approximately half of BD sample taking lithium which may have neuroprotective effects; euthymic patients only so mood state effects not assessed; cortical thickness only, not examining surface area, volume, white matter, or subcortical structures; potential interpretability issues due to complex covariance between cortical thickness, volume, and surface area; no assessment of whether brain-cognition associations independent of clinical characteristics; univariate group comparisons may not capture heterogeneous cognitive abnormalities; normative neuropsychological data limited to matched controls rather than large normative sample

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study is part of the Bipolar Lithium Imaging and Spectroscopy Study (BLISS; Ethics: UK NREC 14/NE/1135), which was originally designed to investigate lithium effects with 1:1:1 split across BD+lithium, BD lithium-naïve, and HC groups. The current analysis merged BD groups for increased power. Previous BLISS publications reported T1-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and lithium imaging data (Smith et al. 2018; Necus et al. 2021). Normative data sources: HCP Young Adult (n=1113, age 28.80±3.70, 22-37y, 54.4%F), OpenBHB (n=3984, age 24.92±14.29, 5-88y, 47.6%F), OASIS-3 (n=542, age 66.18±8.89, 42-95y, 61.8%F), CamCAN (n=644, age 54.75±18.51, 18-88y, 50.8%F), Newcastle University NCL cohort (n=61, age 75.51±6.13, 61-89y, 47.5%F). Total normative sample before QC: n=6344 (age 32.64±19.39, 5-95y, 50.3%F); after removing outliers >5 MAD: n=5977. Cognitive data preprocessing included imputation of 5% missing data using linear regression (BD 4%, HC 8%), winsorization of outliers ±3 SD, and transformations to achieve multivariate normality (d2 correct, d2 FR, DSST: reflect+log; TMT-A, TMT-B: reflect+sqrt). Analysis also performed with untransformed data showed similar pattern with slightly different regional cross-loadings (left insula, right entorhinal, inferior temporal, medial orbitofrontal reaching 0.3 threshold). BD patients recruited via Clinical Research Network from secondary care and via North East Commissioning Service from primary care GP databases. Comorbid psychiatric diagnoses were permissible if BD was primary diagnosis, excluding neurodevelopmental, neurocognitive, neurodegenerative, and substance abuse disorders. MR scans performed at 9am on 3T Philips Achieva scanner; scans lasted 2h for lithium patients, 1h for others. Neuropsychological battery administered in fixed order after comfort break to avoid fatigue: NART, Category Fluency, TMT A&B, DSST original+Symbol Copy, d2 test; battery lasted approximately 50 minutes. All 7 canonical correlations were non-significant (rho range 0.404-0.860, all Pillai's p>0.05). After FDR correction, significant cortical thickness reductions in BD vs normative-HC remained in: bilateral paracentral, precentral, postcentral; left caudal middle frontal, precuneus, cuneus; right insula, pericalcarine.
